question: In C, which statement sets only bit 3 of register reg to 1 without changing the other bits?
explanation: "1 << 3" is 00001000 in binary, a value (mask) with only bit 3 set. ORing (|) it with the register value forces bit 3 to 1 and leaves the other bits as they were. A plain assignment (=) would overwrite the other bits with 0 and break other peripheral settings. Bits are numbered from 0 at the least significant end.
choiceNotes: Correct. OR sets just that bit.
All other bits would become 0.
AND would clear every bit except bit 3.

question: In C, which statement clears only bit 3 of register reg to 0 without changing the other bits?
explanation: "~(1 << 3)" has only bit 3 clear and every other bit set. ANDing (&) with it forces bit 3 to 0, and the other bits, ANDed with 1, stay unchanged. OR to set, AND NOT to clear, XOR (^) to toggle and AND to test are the four basic patterns for manipulating registers in firmware.
choiceNotes: Correct. AND with a mask that has only bit 3 clear.
OR would set every bit except bit 3.
This would clear every bit except bit 3.

question: To toggle an LED output pin bit between on and off each time the code runs, which C statement is correct?
explanation: With exclusive OR (XOR, ^), a bit XORed with 1 flips and with 0 stays the same. So each execution of "port ^= (1 << 5)" toggles only bit 5 between 0 and 1. It is commonly used to blink LEDs. Some microcontrollers have dedicated registers that toggle bits simply by writing to them.
choiceNotes: This always sets the bit; it does not toggle.
Correct. XOR flips the selected bit.
This always clears the bit; it does not toggle.

question: Which C condition correctly tests whether bit 5 of input register in is 1?
choices: if (in == 5)
explanation: "in & (1 << 5)" clears every bit except bit 5, giving 32 (non-zero, true) if bit 5 is 1 and 0 (false) otherwise. In C any non-zero value is true, so it works directly as an if condition. To get exactly 1 or 0, write "(in >> 5) & 1". OR always yields a non-zero result, so it tests nothing.
choiceNotes: The OR result is never zero, so it is always true.
This checks whether the value is 5, unrelated to bit 5.
Correct. It masks off everything except bit 5.

question: The code above rewrites a multi-bit field of register reg. What does it do?
choices: It sets only bit 5
It clears the 3-bit field in bits 4-6 and then writes 5 (binary 101) into it
It multiplies reg by 5 and shifts it left 4 bits
explanation: 0x7 is 111 in binary, so "0x7 << 4" is a mask with bits 4-6 set. ANDing with its inverse clears the field, and ORing with "5 << 4" (101 in bits 4-6) sets the field to 5 while leaving other bits unchanged. This is the standard pattern for updating registers where several bits together encode one setting, such as an operating mode or divider ratio.
choiceNotes: It sets several bits at once.
Correct. It clears the field and then inserts the new value.
It is bit manipulation, not multiplication.

question: While the main code updates a register bit with "reg |= mask;" (read-modify-write), an interrupt handler changes a different bit of the same register. Which pairs the possible problem with a fix correctly?
choices: The handler's change is lost when main writes back; disable interrupts during the update or use dedicated per-bit set/clear registers
The register is permanently damaged; replace the microcontroller
Nothing happens; no fix is needed
explanation: "reg |= mask" is three operations: read the register, OR, and write back. If an interrupt arrives right after the read and the handler changes another bit, main writes back a value based on the stale read, wiping out the handler's change. Disabling interrupts during the operation, or using set and clear registers where only the bits written as 1 change, makes it a single write and avoids the problem.
choiceNotes: Correct. The cause is an interrupt between the read and the write.
The hardware is not damaged; only a value is lost.
A value can be lost.

question: A switch alone is connected to a microcontroller input pin, with no pull-up or pull-down resistor. What can happen while the switch is open?
choices: The pin always reads 1
The pin floats at an undefined level, and noise makes it read 0 and 1 erratically
The microcontroller loses power
explanation: A CMOS input draws almost no current, so with nothing connected its voltage is undefined and noise from nearby signals or even a hand nearby changes the reading. Sitting at an intermediate voltage can also cause shoot-through current in the input circuit, raising power consumption. With a pull-up resistor to the supply, the pin reads 1 when the switch is open and 0 when it closes to ground. Most microcontrollers offer built-in pull-ups.
choiceNotes: With nothing connected, the value is undefined.
Correct. A resistor is needed to hold it at a defined level.
Power is not cut.

question: When using a microcontroller GPIO (general-purpose input/output) pin, what must be configured first?
choices: Whether the pin is used as an input or an output (its direction)
The color of the pin
The name of the programmer who wrote the code
explanation: A GPIO pin can be used as either an input or an output under software control. Configured as an output through the direction register, the value written to the output register becomes the pin voltage; configured as an input, the pin voltage can be read from the input register. Most microcontrollers also let you set pull-ups, the output type (push-pull or open-drain) and whether the pin serves another peripheral.
choiceNotes: Correct. It is set in a direction register.
Pin color is irrelevant.
The programmer's name is irrelevant.

question: What is the phenomenon called in which a mechanical switch's contacts bounce, turning on and off many times in a short period when pressed?
choices: Latch-up
Crosstalk
Contact bounce (chattering)
explanation: When a mechanical switch closes, the metal contacts bounce and turn on and off for a few milliseconds. A microcontroller reads its pins very fast, so counting naively would register one press as several. The bounce is removed in software by waiting and rereading, or in hardware with a capacitor or Schmitt trigger to smooth the waveform. This processing is called debouncing.
choiceNotes: Latch-up is a CMOS fault where large current keeps flowing.
Crosstalk is signal leaking from an adjacent wire.
Correct. A single press may read as several.

question: Which is the most suitable way to remove switch bounce in software?
choices: Read the pin more often and treat any single 1 as a press
Read the pin every few milliseconds and accept a change only after the same value repeats several times
Reboot the microcontroller whenever the switch is pressed
explanation: Bounce settles within a few milliseconds, so reading the pin, say, every 5 ms and declaring a change only after three identical readings ignores the transitions during bouncing. Reading periodically from a timer interrupt avoids blocking other work. Making the delay too long makes the response feel sluggish, so it is tuned to the switch's characteristics.
choiceNotes: That catches every change during the bounce.
Correct. Changes during bouncing are ignored.
Rebooting is unnecessary.

question: A timer counts a 16 MHz clock divided by 16 with a prescaler and raises an interrupt every 1000 counts. What is the interrupt interval?
choices: 1 µs
1 ms
16 ms
explanation: Dividing 16 MHz by 16 gives a 1 MHz timer clock, so one count is 1 µs. An interrupt every 1000 counts gives an interval of 1 µs × 1000 = 1 ms. A prescaler divides a clock that is too fast so the timer can count over a useful range. A 1 ms interrupt is commonly used for timekeeping, reading switches and the RTOS tick.
choiceNotes: 1 µs is the time of a single count.
Correct. 1 µs × 1000 = 1 ms.
The prescaler divides by 16 rather than multiplying.

question: A PWM signal has a period of 1000 counts, with the output high (1) for 250 counts of each period. What is the duty cycle?
explanation: The duty cycle is the fraction of each period during which the output is high: 250 ÷ 1000 = 25%. PWM (pulse-width modulation) adjusts average voltage or power by changing the high time while keeping the period constant. A microcontroller timer switches the output by comparing its counter with a compare value, so it can produce PWM continuously without CPU involvement.
choiceNotes: 75% is the fraction of time the output is low.
A fraction cannot exceed 100%.

question: Which method is commonly used by microcontrollers to adjust LED brightness or motor speed?
choices: Making the power wires thicker or thinner
Temporarily halting program execution
PWM, switching on and off rapidly and varying the fraction of on time
explanation: Driving an LED or motor on and off rapidly with PWM makes the LED appear as bright as its on-time fraction, and the motor, through inertia, turns at a speed set by the average power. The transistor operates fully on or fully off, so it dissipates less heat than at intermediate voltages, giving efficient control. The frequency is chosen so that LED flicker and motor noise are not noticeable.
choiceNotes: Wire thickness is not used for control.
Halting the program does not adjust anything.
Correct. It finely controls the average power.

question: What is the input capture function of a microcontroller timer used for?
choices: To capture and save a screen image
To record the counter value at the instant an input signal changes, precisely measuring pulse width or frequency
To output a PWM signal from a pin
explanation: With input capture, hardware copies the timer counter into a register at the instant the input signal rises or falls. The difference between two captured values gives the pulse width or period. Reading the time in software after an interrupt adds error from processing delays, but this method measures precisely regardless of them. It is used with rotation sensors, ultrasonic rangefinders and the like.
choiceNotes: It has nothing to do with images.
Correct. Hardware records the value at that instant.
PWM output is done by output compare and similar functions.

question: What should be avoided inside an interrupt handler?
choices: Writing 1 to a flag variable to notify the main code
Clearing the bit that indicates the interrupt source
Time-consuming work such as printing long strings with printf or loops that wait for something to happen
explanation: While an interrupt handler runs long, other interrupts cannot be serviced and the main code stalls. printf takes time to finish and may itself rely on interrupts, so it is especially risky. A handler should do only the minimum, such as moving received data into a buffer or setting a flag, and leave heavy work to the main loop or a task. It must also remember to clear the interrupt source bit.
choiceNotes: Notifying main with a short action is good practice.
Without clearing it, the same interrupt fires repeatedly.
Correct. It holds up other interrupts and the main code for a long time.

question: When the program above is compiled with optimization, led_on() may never be called even after the timer interrupt fires. Which pairs the cause with the fix correctly?
choices: The compiler reads flag only once and never rereads it in the loop; declare flag volatile
The interrupt resets flag to 0; make flag a long
An empty loop halts the CPU; put an addition inside the loop
explanation: Looking only at main, the compiler may conclude that nothing in the loop changes flag, load it into a register once and spin on that value. Even when the interrupt handler updates flag in memory, the loop never sees it. Declaring it volatile makes every access read from or write to memory. For multi-byte variables, additional measures are needed to keep accesses from being interrupted midway.
choiceNotes: Correct. It tells the compiler to reread memory every time.
The handler writes 1, and the type is not the cause.
An empty loop does not halt the CPU.

question: On an 8-bit microcontroller, a timer interrupt increments the 32-bit variable ticks, and the main code reads ticks to compute elapsed time. Why is a wildly wrong value occasionally read?
choices: 8-bit microcontrollers cannot use 32-bit variables
The timer interrupt period changes randomly every time
The 32-bit read takes four separate byte accesses, and an interrupt in between can leave some bytes old and some new
explanation: An 8-bit microcontroller reads one byte at a time, so a 32-bit value takes four reads. If, as the value changes from 0x000000FF to 0x00000100, an interrupt arrives after the low byte has been read, the result combines the old low byte (0xFF) with the new upper byte (0x01), giving something like 0x000001FF. It is prevented by disabling interrupts during the read, or by reading twice until two consecutive reads match.
choiceNotes: They can be used, but not read in one access.
The period is constant.
Correct. Disabling interrupts during the read prevents it.

question: What is a characteristic of serial communication with a UART?
choices: The sender drives a clock wire, and the receiver samples data with that clock
No clock wire is used; both sides agree on a communication speed (baud rate), and a start bit marks each character
Many devices share one wire and are selected by address
explanation: A UART communicates asynchronously over two wires, transmit and receive (plus ground). The line idles at 1; a 0 start bit marks the beginning of a character, followed by the data bits and a 1 stop bit at the end. No clock is sent, so both sides must be configured for the same speed, such as 115200 bps. UARTs are commonly used for debug output and for connecting GPS and radio modules.
choiceNotes: That is synchronous communication like SPI.
Correct. It is asynchronous serial communication.
Selecting by address is what I2C and similar do.

question: On a 115200 bps UART using 8 data bits, no parity and 1 stop bit (8N1), roughly how many bytes can be sent per second?
choices: About 14,400 bytes
About 11,500 bytes
About 115,200 bytes
explanation: In 8N1 format, sending one byte of data takes 10 bits: 1 start bit, 8 data bits and 1 stop bit. 115200 ÷ 10 = 11,520, so about 11,500 bytes per second, or roughly 87 µs per byte. Heavy logging can take longer than expected and delay other processing, so the amount of output and the use of buffers need attention.
choiceNotes: That divides by 8, ignoring the start and stop bits.
Correct. Each byte takes 10 bits.
That treats bits as bytes.

question: A small baud-rate mismatch between UART transmitter and receiver can garble characters. Why is the tolerance limited to roughly a few percent?
choices: The receiver aligns on the start bit and then samples each bit's center with its own clock, so the error accumulates over a character and fails once it exceeds half a bit by the last bit
A baud-rate mismatch lowers the transmitter's voltage
UARTs correct mismatches automatically, so there is effectively no limit
explanation: The receiver aligns its timing at the start of the start bit and then counts at its own baud rate, sampling each bit at its center. A speed mismatch makes the sampling error accumulate bit by bit, and if it exceeds half a bit by the stop bit about 10 bits later, the receiver reads the wrong bit. So the combined error of both sides must stay within a few percent, which requires care with less accurate internal oscillators.
choiceNotes: Correct. More than half a bit of drift over about 10 bits causes errors.
Voltage is unrelated.
An ordinary UART does not correct drift within a character.

question: What is a characteristic of SPI communication?
choices: It is asynchronous without a clock, using only two wires
It is synchronous with the master driving the clock, sends and receives simultaneously, and selects devices with chip-select lines
It selects devices by address, so two wires suffice for any number of devices
explanation: SPI is synchronous communication in which, on the clock driven by the master, data flows simultaneously on a master-to-slave line and a slave-to-master line. Each device gets its own chip-select (CS) line, and only the device whose CS is pulled low communicates. Its simplicity allows clocks of tens of MHz, so it often connects fast parts such as flash memory, displays and ADCs.
choiceNotes: That is closer to a UART.
Correct. It is simple and fast.
That describes I2C.

question: Which set of four signals is generally used by SPI?
choices: SDA and SCL, plus power and ground
SCLK (clock), MOSI (master out), MISO (master in) and CS (chip select)
TX and RX, plus RTS and CTS
explanation: In SPI, the master drives the clock on SCLK, sends data on MOSI (master out, slave in) and simultaneously receives data on MISO (master in, slave out). CS selects which slave to talk to, so three slaves need three CS lines. MOSI and MISO are increasingly being renamed, for example COPI and CIPO or SDO and SDI.
choiceNotes: Those are I2C signals.
Correct. Names such as COPI and CIPO are also used now.
Those are UART signals with flow-control lines.

question: When an SPI part is connected but correct data cannot be read, which setting is most worth checking?
choices: Whether the I2C address matches the part
Whether the UART baud rate matches the part
Whether the clock polarity and phase (CPOL and CPHA, the SPI mode) match the part's specification
explanation: SPI has four modes formed by combining the idle level of the clock (CPOL) and which clock edge samples the data (CPHA). If master and part use different modes, sampling is off by half a period, shifting bits or giving undefined values. The mode must be checked in the part's datasheet and the microcontroller's SPI configured to match.
choiceNotes: SPI has no addresses.
SPI does not synchronize via a baud rate.
Correct. Which of the four modes is used depends on the part.

question: What is a characteristic of I2C communication?
choices: Each device needs a dedicated chip-select line
Separate transmit and receive lines allow both directions at once
Several devices share two wires, clock (SCL) and data (SDA), and the partner is selected by address
explanation: I2C is synchronous serial communication that connects several devices with only two wires, SCL and SDA. The master first sends the partner's 7-bit address, and only the device with that address responds. The lines are open-drain, pulled up to 1 by resistors so any device can pull them low. It suits parts where few wires matter more than speed, such as temperature and acceleration sensors and EEPROMs.
choiceNotes: That describes SPI.
I2C is half duplex, sharing one data line.
Correct. Few wires make it easy to attach many sensors.

question: In I2C, how does the receiver of a data byte acknowledge it?
choices: The receiver holds a separate line at 1
During the ninth clock, the receiver pulls SDA low (ACK)
The receiver echoes the same byte back
explanation: In I2C, on the ninth clock after the 8 data bits, the receiver acknowledges by pulling SDA low (ACK). If no one pulls it low, SDA stays at 1 through the pull-up, which is a NACK. If no ACK follows an address, the device may be missing, the wiring broken or the address wrong, which provides a clue when troubleshooting.
choiceNotes: I2C has no separate acknowledge line.
Correct. Not pulling it low is a NACK.
The byte is not echoed back.

question: You want to connect two identical I2C temperature sensors to the same I2C bus, but both have the same address. Which is a correct solution?
choices: Just connect them; the microcontroller will tell them apart automatically
Swap SDA and SCL on one of them
Change one address via its address-select pins, or put them on separate I2C buses
explanation: I2C selects devices by address, so two devices with the same address would respond together and corrupt the communication. Many parts let you change part of the address by tying pins to supply or ground. If that is not possible, use another I2C peripheral on the microcontroller or separate the devices with an I2C bus multiplexer.
choiceNotes: With the same address, both would respond at once.
Swapping the lines would stop communication.
Correct. Addresses must not collide.

question: Which comparison of UART, SPI and I2C is correct?
choices: I2C suits many devices on few wires, SPI suits high speed, and UART suits simply linking two devices
All three always use a clock wire
All three select devices by address
explanation: UART links two devices asynchronously without a clock, with simple wiring and software. SPI is synchronous with a clock and chip selects, enabling tens of MHz, but each added device needs another CS line. I2C connects many devices on two wires but, being open-drain, runs at about 100 kHz to a few MHz. The choice depends on what the parts support, the speed needed and the wire count.
choiceNotes: Correct. They are chosen to fit the use.
UART uses no clock wire.
Only I2C selects by address.

question: What is the difference between polling and interrupts as ways to learn a peripheral's status?
choices: With polling the CPU checks the status repeatedly; with interrupts the peripheral notifies the CPU when the status changes
Polling and interrupts are the same thing
Interrupts are the method where the CPU repeatedly checks the status
explanation: Polling is simple and predictable because checks happen at fixed intervals, but the CPU keeps checking even when nothing happens, wasting time and power. With interrupts the CPU responds only when something changes, so it can do other work or sleep while waiting. If interrupts are extremely frequent, though, their overhead becomes large, so the choice matters.
choiceNotes: Correct. Interrupts let the CPU do other work while waiting.
They work differently.
That describes polling.

question: Which describes the "super loop" structure often seen in microcontroller programs without an OS?
choices: An infinite loop in main calls each task in turn forever, with urgent work handled by interrupts
Each task is a separate process switched by an OS
The microcontroller reboots after each task finishes
explanation: In a super loop, after initialization, a "while (1)" loop keeps calling tasks such as reading sensors, computing and updating a display in order. Time-critical work is done in interrupts, which notify the loop with flags. It needs no OS, uses little memory and is easy to follow. But if one task takes long, everything else is delayed, so an RTOS is considered when the work grows complex.
choiceNotes: Correct. It is simple and suits small microcontrollers.
That is an OS-based structure.
There is no rebooting.

question: What is the main purpose of using an RTOS (real-time operating system) in embedded devices?
choices: To display attractive windows on a screen
To make average processing speed always faster than a PC OS
To switch among multiple tasks by priority so the system can respond within set time limits
explanation: An RTOS divides work into tasks and switches to a higher-priority task as soon as it becomes ready to run. Its purpose is to make sure time-critical work, such as motor control or communication responses, happens reliably within set time limits. It also provides queues for passing data between tasks, mutexes for protecting resources and timed waits. Examples include FreeRTOS, Zephyr and μITRON.
choiceNotes: Displaying graphics is not the main purpose.
Guaranteeing worst-case time matters more than average speed.
Correct. Predictable response times are what matter.

question: In a preemptive RTOS, while a low-priority task is running, a high-priority task receives the data it was waiting for and becomes ready. What generally happens?
choices: The high-priority task waits until the low-priority task finishes on its own
Both tasks stop and the microcontroller reboots
The low-priority task is suspended midway and the high-priority task runs immediately
explanation: In a preemptive RTOS, when an interrupt or similar event makes a higher-priority task ready, the kernel saves and suspends the running low-priority task and switches to the high-priority one. When the high-priority task finishes or blocks, the low-priority task resumes where it left off. This keeps response times for high-priority work short and predictable.
choiceNotes: That is cooperative (non-preemptive) switching.
There is no reboot.
Correct. This is preemption.

question: Which describes priority inversion in an RTOS?
choices: While a high-priority task waits for a resource held by a low-priority task, a medium-priority task preempts the low one and keeps running, so the high task waits a long time
A bug where priority numbers are interpreted backwards
A rule that high-priority tasks always run after low-priority ones
explanation: If a high-priority task waits for a mutex held by a low-priority task, it must wait until the low task releases it. If an unrelated medium-priority task then starts running, it preempts the low task, which cannot release the resource, so in effect the high task is held up by the medium task. On the Mars Pathfinder lander in 1997, this caused repeated system resets.
choiceNotes: Correct. It famously troubled a Mars lander in 1997.
It is not a misinterpretation of numbers.
There is no such rule.

question: Which describes priority inheritance, used to prevent priority inversion?
choices: Lower the high-priority task to the low task's priority
Give all tasks the same priority
Temporarily raise the low-priority task holding a resource to the priority of the high-priority task waiting for it
explanation: With priority inheritance, when a high-priority task starts waiting for a mutex held by a low-priority task, the low task temporarily gets the high task's priority. It then proceeds without being preempted by medium tasks and returns to its original priority on releasing the resource. The high task waits only for the short time the low task uses the resource. Many RTOS mutexes provide this feature.
choiceNotes: That would delay the high task even more.
Priority would lose its meaning.
Correct. It can release the resource without being preempted by medium tasks.

question: In an RTOS, what is the advantage of using a queue (message queue) to pass data from a sensor-reading task to a display task?
choices: Data passing through a queue is encrypted automatically
The receiver can sleep until data arrives, and differences in speed between sender and receiver are absorbed by the queue
Using a queue makes task priorities unnecessary
explanation: Passing data through a shared variable and flag requires guarding against data races and having the receiver check repeatedly. With an RTOS queue, the sender simply puts data in and the receiver waits in a blocked state without using CPU until data arrives. Because several items can be buffered, no data is lost even if the sender is temporarily faster.
choiceNotes: There is no encryption.
Correct. There is also no need to protect a shared variable manually.
Priorities are still needed.

question: What is the difference between hard real-time and soft real-time?
choices: Hard real-time is built only in hardware, soft only in software
Hard real-time is slow and soft real-time is fast
In hard real-time, missing a deadline even once is a system failure; in soft real-time, occasional lateness only degrades quality
explanation: Hard real-time examples include automotive airbag, engine and brake control, where missing a deadline can cause a serious accident. Meeting deadlines even in the worst case must be verified at design time. Soft real-time examples include video and audio playback, where occasional lateness only causes minor glitches. Which category applies greatly changes how rigorous the verification must be.
choiceNotes: It is not about how the system is built.
It is about how strictly deadlines must be met, not speed.
Correct. Airbag and brake control are hard real-time examples.

question: Why is it bad practice to kick (reset) the watchdog timer unconditionally inside a 1 ms timer interrupt handler?
choices: The watchdog may never be touched from inside an interrupt
Even if the main processing hangs in an endless loop, the interrupt keeps running, so the watchdog can no longer detect the fault
Kicking every 1 ms damages the watchdog
explanation: A watchdog resets the microcontroller if it is not kicked within a set time, recovering from runaway code. But a timer interrupt keeps firing even when the main processing has hung, so kicking there unconditionally hides the hang. The basic practice is to confirm that the main loop and each task have completed a normal cycle and kick only when all have checked in.
choiceNotes: There is no such rule.
Correct. Kick only after confirming normal operation.
Frequent kicking does no damage.

question: What is the role of a bootloader in an embedded device?
choices: It runs first at power-on, starting the main firmware or updating it with new firmware
A part for fixing the device's casing
It automatically fixes bugs in the program
explanation: A bootloader is a small program stored at a fixed location in flash that runs first at power-on. Normally it verifies the main firmware and starts it, but it can also receive new firmware over UART, USB, radio and so on and write it to flash. It is usually excluded from updates and protected so that the bootloader itself is never corrupted.
choiceNotes: Correct. It is essential for firmware updates.
It is software, not a mechanical part.
It does not fix bugs automatically.

question: In devices updated over the air (OTA), why is flash divided into two firmware slots (A and B)?
choices: To run the same program in both slots simultaneously for double speed
To use one slot for storing the user's photos
So new firmware can be written to the other slot, and if anything fails the device can still boot from the original slot
explanation: Writing directly over the running firmware leaves the device unbootable if power or communication is lost midway. With two slots, the new firmware is written to the unused slot, verified, and only then is the boot slot switched. If the new version fails to boot, the bootloader reverts to the original slot. It needs twice the flash, but updates become safe.
choiceNotes: They do not run simultaneously.
Both slots are for firmware.
Correct. It keeps a failed update from bricking the device.

question: What is the main purpose of using a microcontroller's sleep mode in a battery-powered embedded device?
choices: To increase processing speed
To stop the CPU and clocks when idle to cut power, waking only when needed, for example on an interrupt
To erase the program
explanation: A device that reads a sensor once every few seconds has nothing to do most of the time. Sleep mode stops the clocks or power to the CPU and unused peripherals, cutting current to the microampere range. A timer or pin-change interrupt wakes it, and it goes back to sleep as soon as the work is done. Deeper sleep draws less current but takes longer to wake and loses more state.
choiceNotes: It is not for speed.
Correct. Battery life improves greatly.
The program is not erased.

question: A sensor device runs at 10 mA for 1% of the time and sleeps at 10 µA for the remaining 99%. What is the closest average current?
choices: About 0.11 mA
About 5 mA
About 10 µA
explanation: The average current is the sum of each current multiplied by its fraction of time: 10 mA × 0.01 = 0.1 mA and 10 µA × 0.99 ≈ 0.0099 mA, about 0.11 mA in total. As here, even a brief active time often dominates the average, so finishing work quickly to sleep sooner and minimizing sleep current both extend battery life.
choiceNotes: Correct. 0.1 mA plus about 0.01 mA.
That averages without weighting by time.
The active current contributes significantly.

question: Why does firmware on small microcontrollers often avoid dynamic memory allocation such as malloc?
choices: Microcontrollers cannot use any C functions
RAM is small, fragmentation can make allocations fail, and allocation time is hard to predict
Dynamically allocated memory survives power-off
explanation: On a microcontroller with only a few KB to a few hundred KB of RAM, repeated allocation and release fragments free space, so a large allocation can fail even though the total is sufficient. In devices running for months, it may eventually fail. Allocation time is also not constant, which suits real-time work poorly. So designs often reserve all needed memory statically at the start.
choiceNotes: C functions are used normally.
Correct. It is especially problematic for devices that run for a long time.
It is lost when power is cut.

question: On a small microcontroller without an MMU, what should be kept in mind about excessive stack use?
choices: The stack grows automatically without limit, so there is nothing to worry about
A stack overflow always shows an error screen
Stack overflow may not be detected immediately and can silently corrupt neighboring data, so avoid deep recursion and large local arrays and estimate usage
explanation: A PC OS places a no-access page beyond the stack to detect overflow, but microcontrollers without an MMU often lack that mechanism, and an overflowing stack silently overwrites whatever variables lie beyond it. The symptoms appear elsewhere, making the cause hard to track down. Developers avoid deep recursion and large local arrays, estimate maximum usage with tools, or write a marker pattern at the stack's end and check whether it has been overwritten.
choiceNotes: Stack size is limited.
There is no mechanism to display an error screen.
Correct. It tends to cause mysterious bugs.

question: A 12-bit A/D converter with a 3.3 V reference reads a value of 2048. What is the closest input voltage?
choices: About 2.05 V
About 3.3 V
About 1.65 V
explanation: A 12-bit A/D converter represents 0 to 3.3 V in 4096 steps. A reading of 2048 is exactly half, so the voltage is 2048 ÷ 4096 × 3.3 V = 1.65 V, with each step about 0.8 mV. Firmware converts readings with "value × reference ÷ 4096", but any error in the reference voltage carries straight into the result, so the reference accuracy matters when precision is needed.
choiceNotes: That reads the value as millivolts.
3.3 V would read about 4095.
Correct. Exactly half of the 4096 steps.

question: When a microcontroller captures many A/D conversion results at regular intervals, what is the advantage of using DMA?
choices: The A/D converter's resolution increases automatically
The input voltage is amplified automatically
The CPU need not read each result in an interrupt; DMA stores them in memory, reducing CPU load
explanation: If the CPU reads each conversion in an interrupt, at tens of thousands of samples per second the interrupt overhead alone consumes much of its time. With DMA, each completed conversion is written in turn into an array in memory, and the CPU is notified only when the array is full. Combined with a timer that triggers conversions, precisely spaced sampling continues without the CPU.
choiceNotes: Resolution is unchanged.
The voltage is unchanged.
Correct. The CPU can process the data in batches later.

question: When representing peripheral registers with C bit-field structs, what needs care?
choices: Bit fields always make programs twice as fast
Bit ordering and similar details of bit fields are implementation-defined, so another compiler may manipulate unintended bits
Bit fields cannot represent values of 8 bits or more
explanation: Bit fields read nicely, but the C standard leaves to the implementation whether bits are allocated from the top or bottom of a unit, how fields crossing boundaries are handled and the access width. Code that works with one compiler may therefore read or write different bits with another compiler or CPU. Headers supplied by microcontroller vendors are usually written with masks and shifts.
choiceNotes: Speed does not necessarily improve.
Correct. Portability needs attention.
Fields of 8 or more bits are possible.

question: On many microcontrollers, what is the advantage of declaring a large table that never changes (such as font data) as const?
choices: It is placed in flash memory and does not consume scarce RAM
The table contents are automatically compressed
The table contents become freely writable at run time
explanation: Microcontrollers often have hundreds of KB of flash for programs but only tens of KB of RAM. A non-const initialized array goes in .data and is copied from flash to RAM at start-up, consuming RAM. Declaring it const lets it stay in flash as read-only data and be read from there. Some microcontrollers require a special attribute to place data in flash.
choiceNotes: Correct. RAM is often much smaller than flash.
Nothing is compressed.
const means it will not be modified.

question: What can be done through debug interfaces such as JTAG and SWD?
choices: Halt or single-step the program on the real board, inspect registers and variables, and program flash
Change the microcontroller's manufacturing process
Automatically translate the program into another language
explanation: JTAG and Arm's SWD connect the on-chip debug circuitry to a debugger on a PC. You can stop at breakpoints to examine variables and registers, step one instruction at a time and program the flash. They reveal internal state even where printf cannot be used. When shipping a product, the debug function may be disabled so that third parties cannot read out the firmware.
choiceNotes: Correct. It is an essential embedded development tool.
It has nothing to do with manufacturing.
It is not a translation function.

question: You want to run a control calculation every 1 ms on a microcontroller without an OS. Which implementation is most suitable?
choices: Set a flag in a 1 ms timer interrupt, and have the main loop perform the calculation when it sees the flag
Insert an empty loop in the main loop that takes roughly 1 ms to create the interval
Reboot the microcontroller after each calculation
explanation: Timing with an empty loop drifts with the duration of other processing and with compiler optimization, so it is inaccurate. A hardware timer counts precisely regardless of processing, so using a 1 ms interrupt as the reference keeps the interval constant. A short calculation can be done directly in the interrupt, but a longer one is better signaled by a flag and done in the main loop so it does not delay other interrupts.
choiceNotes: Correct. A hardware timer gives an accurate interval.
The interval varies with other work and is inaccurate.
Rebooting is unnecessary.

question: What is the role of a microcontroller's brown-out detector (BOD, brown-out reset)?
choices: To reset the microcontroller when the supply voltage drops below what operation requires, preventing unreliable behavior
To turn on an LED when the room gets dark
To raise the supply voltage automatically
explanation: When a draining battery or unstable supply lowers the voltage, the microcontroller's circuits are no longer guaranteed to work, and it may execute instructions incorrectly or write garbage to flash. A brown-out detector holds the microcontroller in reset while the voltage is below a set threshold and lets it start only after the voltage has recovered sufficiently. It is an important feature for protecting data.
choiceNotes: Correct. It also prevents corrupt flash writes and similar.
It is not a light sensor function.
It does not raise the voltage.

question: On a microcontroller with interrupt priorities, a higher-priority interrupt occurs while a lower-priority handler is running. What generally happens (assuming nesting is allowed)?
choices: The low-priority handler is suspended, the high-priority handler runs, and then the low one resumes
The high-priority interrupt is discarded until the low handler finishes
Both handlers execute in parallel on the same CPU at once
explanation: With interrupt priorities, an urgent interrupt is serviced even while another handler is running. For example, if motor overcurrent detection has high priority and communication reception low priority, overcurrent can be handled at once even mid-reception. Arm Cortex-M's NVIC and others provide this mechanism. Interrupts of equal or lower priority wait until the current handler finishes.
choiceNotes: Correct. This is called interrupt nesting.
It is serviced immediately, not discarded.
One CPU executes one thing at a time.
